solution:
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(1+i\):
\(\dfrac{4+3i}{1-i}=\dfrac{(4+3i)(1+i)}{(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}=\dfrac{4+4i+3i+3i^{2}}{2}=\dfrac{1+7i}{2}\).
Answer: \(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{7}{2}i\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}\,i\):
Numerator \(=(\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}\,i)^{2}=5+2\sqrt{15}\,i+3i^{2}=2+2\sqrt{15}\,i\).
Denominator \(=(\sqrt{5})^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}=8\).
\(=\dfrac{2+2\sqrt{15}\,i}{8}\).
Answer: \(\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{4}i\).

Group real and imaginary parts: \((4x+2y)+(-5x+3y)i=10-7i\).
Equating: \(4x+2y=10\) and \(-5x+3y=-7\).
From the first, \(y=5-2x\); substituting, \(-5x+15-6x=-7\Rightarrow -11x=-22\Rightarrow x=2\), so \(y=1\).
Answer: \(x=2,\ y=1\).

\(x+iy=(7-i)(2+3i)=14+21i-2i-3i^{2}=14+19i+3=17+19i\).
Equating real and imaginary parts.
Answer: \(x=17,\ y=19\).

\(x+iy=\dfrac{2+3i}{5+6i}=\dfrac{(2+3i)(5-6i)}{5^{2}+6^{2}}=\dfrac{10-12i+15i-18i^{2}}{61}=\dfrac{28+3i}{61}\).
Equating real and imaginary parts.
Answer: \(x=\dfrac{28}{61},\ y=\dfrac{3}{61}\).

Let \(\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{3}\,i}=a+bi\). Then \(a^{2}-b^{2}=2\) and \(2ab=2\sqrt{3}\), so \(ab=\sqrt{3}\).
\(a=\sqrt{3},\ b=1\) satisfies both: \(3-1=2\) and \(\sqrt{3}\times 1=\sqrt{3}\).
Answer: \(\pm(\sqrt{3}+i)\).

Let \(\sqrt{18i}=a+bi\). Then \(a^{2}-b^{2}=0\) and \(2ab=18\), so \(ab=9\).
\(a^{2}=b^{2}\) with \(ab>0\) gives \(a=b\), and \(a^{2}=9\Rightarrow a=b=3\).
Answer: \(\pm(3+3i)\).

\(r=|8+15i|=\sqrt{8^{2}+15^{2}}=\sqrt{289}=17\).
Both parts are positive, so the amplitude \(\theta\) lies in the first quadrant with \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{15}{8}\), i.e. \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{15}{8}\right)\).
Answer: modulus \(17\), amplitude \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{15}{8}\right)\), polar form \(17(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) where \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{15}{8}\).

\(r=|6-i|=\sqrt{6^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{37}\).
The point \((6,-1)\) lies in the fourth quadrant, so \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{-1}{6}\right)\).
Answer: modulus \(\sqrt{37}\), amplitude \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{-1}{6}\right)\), polar form \(\sqrt{37}(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) where \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{-1}{6}\).

\(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\), so \(r=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{3}{4}}=1\).
\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) give \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
Answer: modulus \(1\), amplitude \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), polar form \(1\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\).

\(\dfrac{-1-i}{\sqrt{2}}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}i\), so \(r=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}}=1\).
\(\cos\theta=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\sin\theta=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) place \(\theta\) in the third quadrant, so \(\theta=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\).
Answer: modulus \(1\), amplitude \(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\), polar form \(1\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right)\).

\(2i=0+2i\), so \(r=\sqrt{0^{2}+2^{2}}=2\).
\(\cos\theta=0\) and \(\sin\theta=1\) give \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Answer: modulus \(2\), amplitude \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), polar form \(2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

\(-3i=0-3i\), so \(r=\sqrt{0^{2}+(-3)^{2}}=3\).
\(\cos\theta=0\) and \(\sin\theta=-1\) give \(\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) (equivalently \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)).
Answer: modulus \(3\), amplitude \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), polar form \(3\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)\).

\(r=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}}=1\).
\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) give \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Answer: modulus \(1\), amplitude \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), polar form \(1\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\).

In Argand's diagram \(a+ib\) is plotted as the point \((a,b)\), the real part along the X-axis and the imaginary part along the Y-axis.
So \(1+2i\) is the point \(A(1,2)\) in the first quadrant, \(2-i\) is \(B(2,-1)\) in the fourth quadrant, \(-3-2i\) is \(C(-3,-2)\) in the third quadrant, and \(-2+3i\) is \(D(-2,3)\) in the second quadrant.
Answer: the four points are \(A(1,2),\ B(2,-1),\ C(-3,-2),\ D(-2,3)\).
diagramNote: Argand plane with X-axis (real) and Y-axis (imaginary) marked from -4 to 4; plot and label the four points A(1,2), B(2,-1), C(-3,-2), D(-2,3), one in each quadrant.

solution:
First \((1-i)(2-i)=2-i-2i+i^{2}=1-3i\).
Then \((1-3i)(3-i)=3-i-9i+3i^{2}=-10i\).
So \(z=\dfrac{5}{-10i}=-\dfrac{1}{2i}=-\dfrac{1}{2i}\times\dfrac{i}{i}=-\dfrac{i}{2i^{2}}=\dfrac{i}{2}\).
The real part of \(z\) is \(0\) and its imaginary part \(\dfrac{1}{2}\ne 0\), hence \(z\) is purely imaginary.
Answer: \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}i\), which is purely imaginary.

\(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{i}{\sqrt{2}}=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\dfrac{i}{\sqrt{2}}=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}-i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
By De Moivre's theorem the first raised to the 10th power is \(\cos\dfrac{10\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{10\pi}{4}=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=i\), and the second is \(\cos\dfrac{10\pi}{4}-i\sin\dfrac{10\pi}{4}=-i\).
Hence the sum is \(i+(-i)=0\).
Answer: the sum is \(0\), as required.

\(\dfrac{1+i}{\sqrt{2}}=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\dfrac{1-i}{\sqrt{2}}=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}-i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
By De Moivre's theorem, \(\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)^{8}=\cos 2\pi+i\sin 2\pi=1\) and \(\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}-i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)^{8}=\cos 2\pi-i\sin 2\pi=1\).
Hence the sum is \(1+1=2\).
Answer: the sum is \(2\), as required.

Rationalise: \(z=\dfrac{(2+6\sqrt{3}\,i)(5-\sqrt{3}\,i)}{5^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\dfrac{10-2\sqrt{3}\,i+30\sqrt{3}\,i-6\cdot 3\,i^{2}}{28}=\dfrac{28+28\sqrt{3}\,i}{28}=1+\sqrt{3}\,i\).
Then \(r=\sqrt{1+3}=2\), and \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2},\ \sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) give \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
Answer: polar form \(2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\); exponential form \(2e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\).

\(r=\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{38}\).
The point \((-6,\sqrt{2})\) lies in the second quadrant, so \(\theta\) is the second-quadrant angle with \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{-6}=\dfrac{-\sqrt{2}}{6}\), i.e. \(\theta=\pi-\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\).
Answer: polar form \(\sqrt{38}(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) where \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{-\sqrt{2}}{6}\); exponential form \(\sqrt{38}\,e^{i\theta}\).

\(r=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{-3}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4}+\dfrac{27}{4}}=3\).
\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{-3/2}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}/2}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(\theta\) is in the second quadrant with \(\tan\theta=-\sqrt{3}\), giving \(\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).
Answer: polar form \(3\left(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\); exponential form \(3e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}\).

\(\sqrt{-3}=\sqrt{3}\,i\), so let \(w=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\).
\(w^{2}=\dfrac{1-2\sqrt{3}\,i+3i^{2}}{4}=\dfrac{-2-2\sqrt{3}\,i}{4}=\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\).
Then \(z=w^{3}=w^{2}\cdot w=\dfrac{(-1-\sqrt{3}\,i)(-1+\sqrt{3}\,i)}{4}=\dfrac{1-3i^{2}}{4}=\dfrac{4}{4}=1\).
(Indeed \(w\) is a complex cube root of unity, so \(w^{3}=1\).)
Answer: \(z=1\), which is a rational number.

\(\dfrac{1-2i}{3-4i}=\dfrac{(1-2i)(3+4i)}{3^{2}+4^{2}}=\dfrac{3+4i-6i-8i^{2}}{25}=\dfrac{11-2i}{25}\).
The second term is its conjugate, \(\dfrac{11+2i}{25}\), since it is obtained by replacing \(i\) by \(-i\).
Adding, the imaginary parts cancel: \(\dfrac{11-2i}{25}+\dfrac{11+2i}{25}=\dfrac{22}{25}\).
Answer: the sum is \(\dfrac{22}{25}\), which is real.

Take out the lowest power from each part:
Numerator \(=i^{230}\left(i^{8}+i^{6}+i^{4}+i^{2}+1\right)=i^{230}(1-1+1-1+1)=i^{230}\).
Denominator \(=i^{220}\left(i^{8}+i^{6}+i^{4}+i^{2}+1\right)=i^{220}\).
So the value is \(\dfrac{i^{230}}{i^{220}}=i^{10}=i^{2}=-1\).
Answer: \(-1\).

The complex cube roots of unity are \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\), with \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\).
Take \(\alpha=\omega,\ \beta=\omega^{2}\). Then \(\alpha^{2}=\omega^{2}\) and \(\beta^{2}=\omega^{4}=\omega\).
So the product is \((1-\omega)(1-\omega^{2})(1-\omega^{2})(1-\omega)=\left[(1-\omega)(1-\omega^{2})\right]^{2}\).
Now \((1-\omega)(1-\omega^{2})=1-\omega-\omega^{2}+\omega^{3}=1-(\omega+\omega^{2})+1=1-(-1)+1=3\).
Hence the product is \(3^{2}=9\).
Answer: \((1-\alpha)(1-\beta)(1-\alpha^{2})(1-\beta^{2})=9\), as required.

\(\dfrac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{-1-i\sqrt{3}}{2}\) are the complex cube roots of unity \(w\) and \(w^{2}\), so \(w^{3}=1\).
\(w^{18}=(w^{3})^{6}=1\) and \((w^{2})^{18}=(w^{3})^{12}=1\).
Hence the sum is \(1+1=2\).
Answer: \(2\).
